sm: Matt Walsh opens by saying new text messages suggest the Cornell 7 were victims of a false narrative that began with the accuser's sorority sisters, who wanted to protect their sorority's reputation. Before getting to that, he turns to Russell Brand's sentencing, where he says the judge praised the bravery of the women who testified and complained that they had been told they lied or agreed to sexual demands. Walsh argues the judge is effectively lecturing a defendant for presenting a defense and cross-examining accusers.

He lists points Brand's lawyers raised: no corroborating evidence beyond the women's claims, events nearly two decades old, no reports at the time, and text messages recounted from memory because they were lost. He notes the jury acquitted on some charges, which he says shows cross-examination worked in part. He argues Brand's ten-year sentence was harsher than those given for some killings, and that the beyond a reasonable doubt standard was ignored because plausible innocent scenarios were never disproved. He adds that Meta deleted Brand's Instagram account, and says this treatment awaits anyone outside the left's preferred groups.

Walsh recaps the Cornell 7 case as he sees it. An adult woman voluntarily took part in group sexual activity at a fraternity house, said afterward in writing that nothing illegal happened, was then disinvited from the Halloween party, and later reframed events as assault. Police found no crime, and two years later a lawsuit made new accusations. He mocks a survey claiming a third of Cornell women experienced non-consensual contact, citing its 13 percent response rate and self-reported, broad definition. He then plays a faculty member describing the no-confidence vote in the administration as a resounding message.

He plays video of a student at the faculty meeting describing campus fears, and argues the left uses incendiary language such as gang rape to make people imagine kidnapping. He reads the accuser's own post-event texts, in which she called the encounter a gang bang, said none of the sexual stuff was illegal, and offered to talk if the men had regrets. Walsh says these are not messages sent to kidnappers, and that the men might have a better claim than she does. He says her tone changed only when she felt her reputation was destroyed.

Walsh continues with the student's complaint that drunk women walk home at night without anyone helping. He questions what help is expected and argues that false accusations make it unwise for any man to assist a drunk woman, saying he would tell his own sons not to. He then plays a professor who says first-year students are terrified, followed by an Asian studies professor who asks whether rape is less destructive than protesting genocide. Walsh calls the question incoherent, says the Cornell 7 did not rape anyone, and contrasts them with Gaza protesters who committed documented crimes.

He goes on to say leftists inject Gaza into every topic, and that he personally does not care about it. He argues students feel unsafe because their teachers tell them to, and that faculty in science and engineering mostly voted against the resolution while humanities faculty led it. He turns to Free Press reporting on new texts showing the sorority pushed an assault narrative to protect its reputation. He reads texts from the day after, where the accuser thanked a man, said everyone was confused and high, and hoped they could joke about it later. He also cites her text about marking it on rice purity, and notes anonymous Greek Rank posts that could have come from anyone.

Walsh reads an October 27th text from the accuser's sorority big sister, who said to shut the rumors down and suggested that if they were true, it would be rape. He reads this as damage control by a sorority whose reputation was suffering, giving the accuser an out. He then covers the October 30th text where the fraternity president disinvited her from the Halloween party and she angrily said she had been uninvited. Her first suggestion of assault came on November 3rd, followed by an emergency room visit. He notes that Attorney General Letitia James stepped aside the day after the midterms and calls the case a political and PR operation. He says the legal system lets accusers change their story, and calls for reforms such as letting defendants cross-examine accusers about their history and name them, plus equal punishment for false accusers. He closes by urging men to avoid casual encounters and college campuses.
